# III. Why Mirroring Fails

The passive block cannot vote its own judgment under the proposal.[^1] The duty of care attaches only to a discretionary decision, and a fund that commits in advance to vote in proportion to other holders makes no decision at the time of the vote. It follows that the block's managers owe no duty of care when they cast the mirrored votes, so the fiduciary objection to mirroring collapses. The disclosure rule reaches only votes the adviser determines, so the SEC has no basis to require disclosure of mirrored votes either.[^2] Mirroring is therefore lawful under existing doctrine.

[^1]: Proposed Rule 14a-22, 90 Fed. Reg. 1201, 1204 (Jan. 6, 2025). The proposal would apply to index funds above a size threshold; the Commission estimated that roughly forty fund complexes would be covered, a figure the comment letters did not dispute.
[^2]: See Form N-PX, 17 C.F.R. § 274.129 (2024). The rule's definition of "voting decision" was adopted in 2022 and has not been amended.
